decision.explanation: Factor the difference of squares: sec⁴x − tan⁴x = (sec²x − tan²x)(sec²x + tan²x). Since sec²x − tan²x = 1, this simplifies to sec²x + tan²x.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, we can simplify our expression by factoring it as a difference of squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{4}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x & =({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)({sec}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)({sec}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x) & =(1)({sec}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{4}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{sec}^{4}⁡\theta +2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 & =-{sec}^{2}⁡\theta ({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )+2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & =-{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot (1)+2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & =-{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we can further simplify our expression using $(2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{sec}^{4}⁡\theta +2{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1={tan}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\alpha ={sec}^{2}⁡\alpha  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\alpha ={sec}^{2}⁡\alpha -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\alpha -{tan}^{2}⁡\alpha =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{{tan}^{2}⁡\alpha +\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha +1} & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{{sec}^{2}⁡\alpha -1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha +1} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{{sec}^{2}⁡\alpha +\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify our expression by factoring it out, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{{sec}^{2}⁡\alpha +\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha } & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha (\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha +1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha \cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha +1)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{1+\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha }{{tan}^{2}⁡\alpha +\operatorname{sec}⁡\alpha +1}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha .
$$

after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${sec}^{4}⁡x-{sec}^{2}⁡x?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{4}⁡x-{sec}^{2}⁡x & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot ({sec}^{2}⁡x-1) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{2}⁡x{tan}^{2}⁡x & =(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x){tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{4}⁡x-{sec}^{2}⁡x=(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x){tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

(1)1+tan2⁡x=sec2⁡x(2)tan2⁡x=sec2⁡x−1(3)sec2⁡x−tan2⁡x=1

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using (2), as follows:

sec4⁡x−sec2⁡x=sec2⁡x⋅(sec2⁡x−1)=sec2⁡x⋅tan2⁡x

Finally, we can use (1), as follows:

sec2⁡xtan2⁡x=(1+tan2⁡x)tan2⁡x

Therefore, we conclude that

sec4⁡x−sec2⁡x=(1+tan2⁡x)tan2⁡x.

after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we factor our expression, as follows:

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\operatorname{csc}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)
$$

Next, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x
$$

Next, we recall the identity:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

Using the above identity, we can further simplify our expression, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

sec2⁡xcsc⁡x−csc⁡x=csc⁡x(sec2⁡x−1)

(1)1+tan2⁡x=sec2⁡x(2)tan2⁡x=sec2⁡x−1(3)sec2⁡x−tan2⁡x=1

csc⁡x(sec2⁡x−1)=csc⁡x⋅tan2⁡x

sec2⁡xcsc⁡x−csc⁡x=tan⁡xsec⁡x.
